META.subject: Mathematics
META.subtitleDoc: CBE Phenomenon-Driven Lesson Sequence — Sub-Strand 1.3 (7 Lessons)

UNIT.subject: Mathematics
UNIT.content:
• Quadratic expressions: identifying, expanding, and simplifying expressions of the form ax² + bx + c
• Factorisation of quadratic expressions (including difference of two squares and perfect squares)
• Forming quadratic equations from real-life contexts (e.g., area problems, Harambee fundraising targets)
• Solving quadratic equations by factorisation
• Solving quadratic equations by completing the square
• Solving quadratic equations using the quadratic formula
• Applications of quadratic equations in day-to-day situations
UNIT.learningOutcomes:
By the end of the sub-strand, the learner should be able to:
a) identify and write quadratic expressions of the form ax² + bx + c in different situations,
b) expand and simplify quadratic expressions using algebraic rules,
c) factorise quadratic expressions including perfect squares and difference of two squares,
d) form quadratic equations from real-life contexts such as area, fundraising, and motion,
e) solve quadratic equations by factorisation,
f) solve quadratic equations by completing the square,
g) solve quadratic equations using the quadratic formula,
h) apply quadratic equations to solve problems in day-to-day situations,
i) appreciate the relevance of quadratic equations in modelling real-world phenomena.
UNIT.coreCompetencies:
• Communication and Collaboration: The learner discusses with peers to expand, simplify, and factorise quadratic expressions, and shares solution strategies for equations derived from real-life Harambee fundraising and farming contexts.
• Critical Thinking and Problem Solving: The learner analyses real-life situations (e.g., calculating the dimensions of a shamba plot in Kericho given its area) to form and solve quadratic equations, selecting the most efficient method among factorisation, completing the square, or the quadratic formula.
• Digital Literacy: The learner uses calculators and digital devices to verify solutions to quadratic equations and explore graphical representations of quadratic functions.
• Learning to Learn: The learner reflects on errors in algebraic manipulation and refines personal strategies for solving quadratic equations across multiple methods.
• Self-Efficacy: The learner builds confidence by successfully modelling and solving progressively complex quadratic problems rooted in Kenyan everyday contexts.
UNIT.values:
• Unity: The learner works collaboratively in groups to explore and compare different methods of solving quadratic equations, appreciating diverse approaches.
• Responsibility: The learner takes responsibility for accuracy in algebraic working, understanding that errors in quadratic modelling (e.g., miscalculating a land area or fundraising shortfall) have real consequences.
• Integrity: The learner honestly records and presents their working, showing all steps in solving quadratic equations rather than copying answers.
• Social Justice: The learner recognises how mathematical literacy, including understanding quadratic relationships, empowers community members to make fair and informed decisions about resources and fundraising.
UNIT.sep:
• Asking Questions and Defining Problems: Students pose mathematical questions about what dimensions or quantities satisfy a given quadratic constraint (e.g., "What side length gives exactly 96 m² for the Harambee hall floor?").
• Developing and Using Models: Students build and revise algebraic models (quadratic equations) to represent real-life situations, updating their models as new constraints are introduced.
• Using Mathematics and Computational Thinking: Students apply factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula as computational tools to obtain exact solutions, and use calculators to verify numerical answers.
• Constructing Explanations: Students explain why a quadratic equation may have two, one, or no real solutions, connecting algebraic reasoning to the physical sense of the context (e.g., rejecting negative lengths).
• Engaging in Argument from Evidence: Students compare solution methods and justify which method is most efficient for a given quadratic equation, supporting their argument with worked examples.
UNIT.pcis:
• Life Skills (Critical Thinking and Problem Solving): The learner applies quadratic equations to analyse and solve real-life problems such as determining optimal dimensions for a community hall or maximising a farming plot's area in the Rift Valley.
• Financial Literacy: The learner uses quadratic equations to model fundraising scenarios, such as calculating contribution amounts or shortfalls in a Harambee event, developing awareness of financial planning.
• Environmental Education: The learner connects quadratic area models to land use and conservation contexts, such as calculating the area of irrigation plots along Lake Victoria to avoid over-use of resources.
• Citizenship: The learner appreciates how mathematics supports equitable community development decisions, such as fair allocation of land or Harambee funds.
UNIT.careers:
• Architecture and Civil Engineering: Quadratic equations are used to calculate structural dimensions, load distributions, and areas of buildings — directly relevant to constructing community halls, schools, and housing in Nairobi and beyond.
• Agriculture and Land Management: Farmers and land surveyors in the Rift Valley use quadratic area models to optimise field layouts, irrigation coverage, and crop yield planning.
• Finance and Accounting: Financial analysts and accountants use quadratic and polynomial models to project revenue targets, model loan repayments, and analyse cost-profit relationships.
• Physics and Engineering: Quadratic equations model projectile motion, enabling careers in mechanical engineering, aerospace, and sports science (e.g., analysing the trajectory of a javelin thrown by a Kenyan athlete).
• Data Science and Information Technology: Programmers and data scientists use quadratic and higher-order functions in algorithm optimisation, machine learning cost functions, and computer graphics rendering.
UNIT.focus: This unit develops learners' ability to work fluently with quadratic expressions and equations, moving from conceptual understanding of the algebraic structure ax² + bx + c through to practical solution methods and real-world application. Using the anchoring context of a community Harambee fundraising challenge in a Kenyan village, learners discover that some real-life problems cannot be solved with linear equations alone, motivating the need for quadratic thinking. Across seven lessons, learners progress from recognising and forming quadratic expressions, through three distinct solution methods (factorisation, completing the square, and the quadratic formula), to critically applying their skills in authentic Kenyan contexts such as land area calculations, construction planning, and financial modelling.
UNIT.phenomenon: A community in Githurai, Nairobi, is planning a Harambee to raise funds to build a new multipurpose hall. The organising committee knows the hall must have a rectangular floor with an area of exactly 120 m², and that the length must be 2 metres more than the width. When the committee tries to find the dimensions using simple arithmetic or a linear equation, they get stuck — no straightforward linear method gives them an answer. A local Form 4 student suggests the problem requires a quadratic equation. Students are shown the committee's hand-drawn sketch on a manila paper: a rectangle labelled "width = w" and "length = w + 2", with "Area = 120 m²" written in the centre. The puzzle is immediately visible: how can you find a single unknown when it appears multiplied by itself? Students are asked to predict the width before any instruction is given, and most guesses are either wrong or arrived at by trial-and-error — revealing the limitation of their current tools and creating genuine need for the new mathematics of this unit.
UNIT.supportingPhenomena:
• A maize farmer in Kericho wants to fence a rectangular plot along one side of a river (so only three sides need fencing). She has exactly 60 metres of wire and wants the enclosed area to be 400 m². Students discover that forming the area constraint produces a quadratic equation, and that it may have two possible solutions — only one of which is physically sensible.
• A mandazi vendor at Gikomba Market in Nairobi prices her mandazi at Ksh x per piece. She notices that when she raises the price by Ksh 5, the number of mandazis she sells per day drops by 10, yet her total revenue stays at Ksh 2,000. Students form a quadratic equation to find the original price, encountering a real-life revenue model.
• A stone is thrown vertically upward from the top of a building in Mombasa. Its height above the ground (in metres) after t seconds is given by h = −5t² + 20t + 25. Students use the quadratic formula to find when the stone hits the ground, connecting quadratic equations to motion in a physical context they can visualise.
• A Nakuru school wants to create a rectangular garden inside a 10 m × 8 m courtyard, leaving a uniform path of width x metres around it. The garden area must be 48 m². Students model the situation as a quadratic equation in x, reinforcing how quadratic equations arise naturally from geometric constraints.
UNIT.drivingQuestion:
DRIVING QUESTION: How can we use quadratic equations to find unknown dimensions and quantities that help our community solve real planning problems — like building the Harambee hall in Githurai?

KICD KEY INQUIRY QUESTIONS:
1. How do quadratic expressions and equations differ from linear ones, and why are they necessary?
2. How can we use quadratic equations to model and solve problems in day-to-day activities?
UNIT.storylineThread:
Lesson 1 — PREDICT & ANCHOR PHENOMENON: Students examine the Githurai Harambee hall problem. They predict the hall dimensions using trial-and-error and discuss why linear equations fall short. The class co-constructs the equation w(w + 2) = 120, identifying it as a new type of equation. Students are introduced to the general form ax² + bx + c = 0 and begin recognising quadratic expressions in varied contexts. The Driving Question Board (DQB) is opened and initial "What we notice / What we wonder" cards are posted.

Lesson 2 — EXPANDING & SIMPLIFYING QUADRATIC EXPRESSIONS: Students learn to expand products such as (w + 2)(w + 3) and (2x − 1)(3x + 4) using the distributive law and FOIL method. Supporting phenomena (the Kericho farm fencing problem) is introduced to show how real contexts generate quadratic expressions. Students simplify expressions and begin to see the structure of ax² + bx + c emerging consistently. DQB is updated: "We now know how quadratic expressions are formed."

Lesson 3 — FACTORISATION OF QUADRATIC EXPRESSIONS: Students reverse the expansion process to factorise quadratic expressions of the form x² + bx + c and ax² + bx + c, including perfect square trinomials and difference of two squares. Using the Harambee hall equation (w² + 2w − 120 = 0), students practise factorising and identify factors that correspond to real dimensions. The Gikomba mandazi revenue problem is introduced as a factorisation challenge. DQB update: "Factorisation lets us 'undo' expansion to find hidden values."

Lesson 4 — SOLVING QUADRATIC EQUATIONS BY FACTORISATION: Students formally solve quadratic equations by setting each factor equal to zero (Zero Product Property). They apply this to the Harambee hall problem, obtaining w = 10 and w = −12, then reason about which solution is physically valid. Multiple Kenyan-context equations are solved in pairs. Students revisit the DQB and refine their model: "A quadratic equation can have two solutions; context tells us which one to use."

Lesson 5 — SOLVING BY COMPLETING THE SQUARE: Students are introduced to completing the square as a method for equations that do not factorise easily. Using the Nakuru school garden problem (x² + ... = 48), they practise transforming quadratic equations into the form (x + p)² = q and solving. The geometric interpretation (literally completing a square diagram) is drawn to connect algebra to area. DQB update: "Completing the square always works, even when factorisation fails."

Lesson 6 — THE QUADRATIC FORMULA & THE MOMBASA STONE PROBLEM: Students derive the quadratic formula by completing the square on the general form ax² + bx + c = 0. They apply it to the Mombasa projectile problem (−5t² + 20t + 25 = 0) and the mandazi pricing problem, comparing results to earlier methods. Students use calculators to verify solutions and discuss the discriminant (b² − 4ac) to determine the number of real solutions. DQB update: "The quadratic formula is a universal tool — it works for any quadratic equation."

Lesson 7 — APPLICATION, MODEL BUILDING & CONSOLIDATION: Students return to the full Harambee hall scenario and present complete solutions using all three methods, justifying their preferred approach. New application problems (land area, fundraising revenue, construction) are solved in groups. Students construct a final cumulative model (poster or digital slide) mapping the journey from recognising quadratic expressions to solving equations in context. The DQB is formally closed — all initial "wonder" questions are answered. Students reflect on how quadratic thinking empowers community problem-solving.

LESSONS.title: Predict & Anchor Phenomenon: The Githurai Harambee Hall
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; double period optional for DQB)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: quadratic equation, unknown multiplied by itself, w(w + 2) = 120, general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0, coefficients a, b, c, linear equation, trial and error, Driving Question Board, Githurai Harambee hall

slo.purpose: To launch the unit by confronting learners with the Githurai Harambee hall problem, so they feel the limits of arithmetic and linear equations and discover the need for quadratic equations.
slo.knowledge: Learners will recognise that when an unknown is multiplied by itself (w x w), the equation contains a w^2 term and is quadratic, not linear. They will form w(w + 2) = 120, write it as w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0, state the general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not equal to 0), and identify a = 1, b = 2, c = -120 for the hall equation.
slo.skills: Making predictions and testing them with a trial-and-error table (w = 8 to 12); modelling a real situation with an equation (NGSS-style SEP: developing and using models, asking questions); comparing linear and quadratic situations (perimeter 4w + 4 versus area); communicating reasoning in pairs and writing What we notice / What we wonder cards.
slo.attitudes: Curiosity and perseverance when current tools are not enough; unity and collaboration in pairs and groups; appreciation that mathematics helps communities plan, as in a Harambee.
slo.keyInquiry: How do quadratic expressions and equations differ from linear ones, and why are they necessary? (Also opens: How can we use quadratic equations to model and solve problems in day-to-day activities?)
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 anchors the whole unit. Learners meet the Githurai hall, predict the width, and create a need to know. They end with the equation w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0 and an open DQB. Lesson 2 will build on the general form and on w(w + 2) to learn expansion with FOIL. The equation is NOT solved formally here; solving methods come in later lessons.
slo.safetyNotes: Low-risk classroom lesson. Keep aisles clear when groups move to the DQB wall. Use tape or sticky tack for cards, and have learners stand safely when posting. Share manila paper and markers carefully.

LESSONS.overview: Learners are shown the Githurai committee's manila-paper sketch: a rectangle labelled width = w, length = w + 2, Area = 120 m^2. They predict the width and explain how they got it. Most guesses come from trial and error. The class tests guesses in a table (w = 8 to 12), finds that w = 10 gives exactly 120 m^2 but that nobody could be sure without testing, and asks why a linear equation like the perimeter 4w + 4 cannot give area. Through Think-Pair-Share, learners build w(w + 2) = 120 and rewrite it as w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0. The teacher introduces the general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 and learners identify a = 1, b = 2, c = -120, then sort expressions as linear or quadratic. The class opens the Driving Question Board with What we notice / What we wonder cards and makes a first model sketch.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners view the committee's manila-paper sketch (rectangle, width = w, length = w + 2, Area = 120 m^2) with the story: the Githurai community is planning a Harambee to raise funds for a new multipurpose hall, and the committee is stuck. Individually, each learner writes in their exercise book a prediction of the width in metres, with one sentence on how they got it. Then they try to write a linear equation for the problem and note why it fails. Learners share in pairs and record their predictions on a class tally on the board.
framework.teacherMoves: Display or draw the sketch on the board. Say: "The Githurai committee wants a hall floor of exactly 120 square metres, with the length 2 metres more than the width. They tried arithmetic and linear equations and got stuck. Before I teach anything, what do you think the width is?" Give 1 minute of silent writing. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, "What would a linear equation look like here?" Cold-call 4 learners for predictions and record all on the board without saying whether they are right. Ask 2 learners: "How did you get your number?" Say: "Wrong guesses are welcome today; they help us see what tools we need."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Reveal (Prediction Tally): Making a prediction before instruction activates prior knowledge of area of a rectangle and linear equations, and exposes the limits of those tools. The visible tally of different guesses creates a shared puzzle and a genuine need for new mathematics.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners write a numerical prediction with a reason; (2) learners link area to length x width; (3) at least some say they used guess-and-check; (4) learners attempt a linear equation and cannot produce one. Record the range of predictions and any misconceptions (e.g. 120 divided by 2 = 60, or adding w + w + 2 = 120).

framework.learnerExperience: In pairs, learners test guesses by completing a trial-and-error table for w = 8, 9, 10, 11, 12 with columns: width w, length w + 2, area w x (w + 2), and comment. They find: w = 8, l = 10, 80 m^2 (too small); w = 9, l = 11, 99 m^2 (too small); w = 10, l = 12, 120 m^2 (exact); w = 11, l = 13, 143 m^2 (too big); w = 12, l = 14, 168 m^2 (too big). They then compute the perimeter 2(w + w + 2) = 4w + 4 and notice that it is linear and does not give the area. Finally, they notice that w appears multiplied by itself when writing the area.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out the table template or have learners rule it in their books. Circulate and ask: "What happens to the area as w grows from 8 to 12? Does it grow by the same amount each time?" (Differences: 19, 21, 23, 25.) Cold-call 3 pairs to report which row gave exactly 120. Say: "Trial and error worked here, but what if the numbers were not whole? What if the committee had no time to test?" WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, "Why can't the perimeter 4w + 4 tell us the area?" Then ask: "Look at area = w x (w + 2). What do you notice about w?" Guide towards w x w = w^2.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern Noticing with a Data Table: Learners see the area changing by unequal amounts (19, 21, 23, 25), unlike the steady change of a linear relationship. Comparing the perimeter 4w + 4 (constant rate of change) with the area builds an evidence-based distinction between linear and non-linear relationships.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check tables for correct products (80, 99, 120, 143, 168). Look for learners who: identify w = 10 as the match; state that the area increases by growing amounts; correctly compute the perimeter 4w + 4; and say that w x w gives a squared term. Ask 2 learners to explain in one sentence why the perimeter is linear and the area is not.

framework.learnerExperience: Using Think-Pair-Share, learners write the equation for the hall: w(w + 2) = 120. They expand using the distributive law in a simple way (w x w + w x 2) to write w^2 + 2w = 120, then move 120 to the left to get w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0. The teacher introduces the general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 (a not equal to 0), and learners label a = 1, b = 2, c = -120. They then classify given expressions and equations as linear or quadratic, e.g. 4w + 4, w^2 + 2w - 120, 3x - 7 = 0, 2x^2 - 5x + 1 = 0, and give a reason (highest power 2 versus 1). They explain in their own words why the hall problem needs a quadratic equation.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Let's write down exactly what the committee knows. Area is length times width. Turn to your partner and write an equation using w." WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after the question, then cold-call 3 pairs. Write w(w + 2) = 120 on the board. Say: "Remove the bracket: w times w is w squared, w times 2 is 2w." Show w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0. Introduce vocabulary: "An expression whose highest power is 2 is a quadratic expression; set equal to something, it is a quadratic equation. The general form is ax^2 + bx + c = 0, where a is not zero." Ask: "Why can't a be zero?" (Cold-call 2.) Ask 3 learners to state a, b and c for the hall. Do not solve the equation yet; say: "We will learn how to expand, factorise and solve in the coming lessons. Today we name the problem." Show 6 mixed expressions for quick linear/quadratic sorting using thumbs up or down.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Vocabulary Building: Learners claim the hall equation is quadratic and support it with evidence from the table and the w x w term. Naming a, b, c connects the concrete hall problem to a general structure, which supports transfer to later contexts.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: correct equation w(w + 2) = 120; correct rearrangement to w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0; correct a = 1, b = 2, c = -120 (watch for the sign of c); correct linear/quadratic sorting with reasons. Use a 3-question exit check: (1) State a, b, c in 3x^2 - 4x + 5 = 0. (2) Is 5w + 10 quadratic? Why? (3) Why is the hall equation not linear?

framework.learnerExperience: Groups of 4 write What we notice cards (e.g. area changes by 19, 21, 23, 25; w x w gives w^2; the perimeter is linear) and What we wonder cards (e.g. Is there a quick way to find w without guessing? Can there be two answers? What if the answer is not a whole number? Can a width be negative? How do we find unknown dimensions for other community plans?). They post cards on the DQB under the driving question: How can we use quadratic equations to find unknown dimensions and quantities that help our community solve real planning problems, like building the Harambee hall in Githurai? Learners group similar cards into themes.
framework.teacherMoves: Write the driving question on a manila-paper banner at the top of the board or wall. Say: "Each group, write at least two notice cards and two wonder cards. One idea per card." Circulate and prompt: "What surprised you? What would the committee need to know?" WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, "Which wonder cards go together?" Cold-call 4 groups to read one card each and place it on the board. Cluster cards into themes such as solving methods, number of solutions, non-whole numbers and other uses. Say: "We will return to this board after every lesson and move cards from wonder to answered."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board (Notice/Wonder Cards): Posting learner-generated questions gives ownership of the learning path and makes curiosity visible. Clustering questions into themes lets learners see how the unit's lessons will answer them.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check cards for specificity and relevance: do wonder cards ask about solving methods, the number of solutions, or applications? Look for learners who link observations to the table or equation. Note questions that foreshadow later lessons (e.g. the negative width, or non-whole answers) and record them as indicators of readiness.

framework.learnerExperience: Each group starts a cumulative model poster on manila paper titled Githurai Hall Model v1. They draw the hall rectangle with width = w, length = w + 2 and Area = 120 m^2. Beside it they write: w(w + 2) = 120, w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0, general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a = 1, b = 2, c = -120. They add a box: Linear: highest power 1 (perimeter 4w + 4); Quadratic: highest power 2 (area). Below, they write What we still need to find out, with 2 open questions. Learners complete a summary table of what they observed, learned and explained.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: "Your model must show the picture, the equation, the general form and one sentence on why this problem is quadratic and not linear." Circulate and check that c = -120 has the right sign. WAIT TIME: 10-15 seconds after asking, "What is the one thing our current model cannot do yet?" (Answer: give the width without guessing.) Cold-call 3 groups to share their open questions. Keep posters for revision in each later lesson. Close by saying: "Tomorrow we learn to expand brackets like (w + 2)(w + 3), the first tool for working with quadratics."
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Building: A visual poster that combines diagram, equation and general form helps learners connect representations. Marking the gaps (What we still need) creates a clear target for the next lessons, and the model will be revised in each lesson until Lesson 7.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each poster for: correct labelled sketch; w(w + 2) = 120; w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0; correct a, b, c; a clear linear/quadratic contrast; at least 2 open questions. Look for learners who explain the model to a visitor from another group. Use the summary table to see whether learners can separate what they observed (table, w x w) from what they learned (general form) and explained (why linear fails).

LESSONS.teacherReflection: Which learners relied only on guess-and-check, and who tried to build an equation? Did learners confuse w + w + 2 = 120 or the perimeter with area, and how did I address it? Was the sign of c = -120 a common error? Did the wait time (10-15 seconds) give quieter learners a chance to speak, and did I cold-call a balanced mix? Which wonder cards (e.g. negative width, non-whole answers, two solutions) show readiness to be taken up in later lessons, and how will I highlight them on the DQB? What would I change in the time spent on the trial-and-error table versus the DQB creation?

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe about the Githurai hall problem? Record the trial-and-error table results (w = 8 to 12 and areas 80, 99, 120, 143, 168 m^2), the finding that w = 10 gives exactly 120 m^2, that the area grows by different amounts, and that the perimeter 4w + 4 is linear.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Record that when an unknown is multiplied by itself we get a w^2 term and a quadratic equation; the general form ax^2 + bx + c = 0 with a not equal to 0; and that for the hall w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0, a = 1, b = 2, c = -120.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How can we explain why the committee got stuck? Write 2-3 sentences using the evidence: area = w(w + 2) has w x w, so it is not linear; the perimeter 4w + 4 is linear but does not give area; guessing works only if we are lucky, so we need new methods for quadratic equations.

LESSONS.title: Expanding and Simplifying Quadratic Expressions: From the Githurai Hall to the Kericho Tea Farm
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (one lesson; extend to a double lesson if learners need more practice time)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: expand, distributive law, FOIL, binomial, like terms, quadratic expression, ax^2 + bx + c, coefficient, area model, perimeter, Kericho tea farm

slo.purpose: Learners expand a product of two binomials using the distributive law and FOIL, collect like terms to write the result in the form ax^2 + bx + c, and explain why an area gives a quadratic expression while a perimeter gives a linear one.
slo.knowledge: Learners know that (w + 2)(w + 3) = w^2 + 5w + 6 and (2x - 1)(3x + 4) = 6x^2 + 5x - 4. They know that the area of the Kericho tea-farm plot (x + 5)(x + 3) = x^2 + 8x + 15 m^2 is quadratic, while its fencing perimeter 4x + 16 m is linear. They know that expanding always produces the structure ax^2 + bx + c, with a, b and c identified.
slo.skills: Expanding using the distributive law and FOIL; collecting like terms; checking an expansion by substituting a value (x = 5 gives 80 m^2); drawing and reading an area model; identifying a, b and c; constructing and explaining a mathematical argument (NGSS-aligned practices: using mathematics, constructing explanations, analysing patterns).
slo.attitudes: Learners show precision with signs, persevere when a negative term causes an error, respect peers' reasoning in pair work, and appreciate that algebra helps farmers and committees plan.
slo.keyInquiry: How do quadratic expressions and equations differ from linear ones, and why are they necessary? (KICD Key Inquiry 1) Supporting question: Where do quadratic expressions come from in real planning problems, such as the Githurai Harambee hall and a Kericho tea-farm plot?
slo.purposeInStoryline: In Lesson 1 learners met the Githurai hall expression w(w + 2) and the general form ax^2 + bx + c, and saw that the unknown multiplied by itself makes a quadratic. This lesson teaches how a product of two binomials is expanded and simplified into that general form, so that learners see ax^2 + bx + c emerging every time. This prepares for Lesson 3, where they reverse the process by factorising. The DQB is updated with: 'We now know how quadratic expressions are formed.'
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Use blunt scissors and paper only when cutting area-model rectangles. Keep walkways clear when learners move to gallery-walk stations. Ensure group work is inclusive so every learner can see the manila paper and area models.

LESSONS.overview: Learners begin by recalling the Githurai committee's manila-paper sketch with w(w + 2) = 120 and predict what happens when a similar rectangle has both sides written as brackets: a Kericho tea farmer fences a plot of length (x + 5) m and width (x + 3) m. In the Observe Phase, learners build area models with paper rectangles, then expand (w + 2)(w + 3) with the distributive law and FOIL, and compare area (quadratic) with perimeter (linear). In the Explain Phase they expand (2x - 1)(3x + 4), check results by substitution at x = 5 (80 m^2), and explain how the signs and coefficients behave. They update the DQB with 'What we notice / What we wonder' cards and add a first layer to the cumulative model poster: area of a rectangle with unknown sides leads to ax^2 + bx + c.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the committee's manila-paper sketch from Lesson 1 (width = w, length = w + 2, Area = 120 m^2) and then see a new sketch from a Kericho tea farmer: a rectangular plot with length (x + 5) m and width (x + 3) m. Individually, for 2 minutes, they write on a mini-whiteboard or in their exercise book: (a) 'What will the area expression look like when I multiply (x + 5)(x + 3)? Will it have an x^2 term?' (b) 'What will the fencing perimeter look like? Will it have an x^2 term?' They also predict the area if x = 5. Then they share with a partner and record one prediction and one reason on a sticky note.
framework.teacherMoves: Display both sketches. Say: 'In Lesson 1 we saw that w times (w + 2) gave us a w squared. Today a Kericho tea farmer wants to fence a plot, and both sides have brackets. Before I teach you anything, what do you think the area will look like?' Ask learners to write independently. WAIT TIME: 15 seconds of silence after posing the question before anyone speaks. Cold-call 3 learners (not volunteers) to share predictions, and ask each: 'What makes you think so?' Ask 2 learners to share their prediction for x = 5. Record all predictions on the board without judging them as right or wrong. Say: 'Keep your sticky note; we will come back to it at the end.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Observe-Explain with a Think-Pair-Share: committing to a prediction first makes learners' current thinking visible (for example, 'just add the brackets') and creates a need for a method. Linking to the Githurai hall keeps the new idea tied to the anchoring phenomenon.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners mention an x^2 term for area and not for perimeter. Look for these indicators: (1) at least 3 of 5 observed pairs write a prediction with a reason; (2) note the number of learners who predict x^2 + 15 or 2x + 8 (a common misconception: multiplying only the first and last terms); (3) tally the predicted values for x = 5 on the board. Use the tally to plan which misconceptions to address in the Observe Phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A (area model, about 8 minutes): In pairs, learners use a pre-drawn grid or cut paper pieces to build the rectangle (w + 2) by (w + 3): one big w by w square, 3 strips of w by 1, 2 strips of 1 by w, and 6 unit squares (2 by 3). They count the pieces and write the total area as w^2 + 3w + 2w + 6. Part B (about 7 minutes): Using the same pieces, they link each piece to FOIL: First w x w = w^2, Outer w x 3 = 3w, Inner 2 x w = 2w, Last 2 x 3 = 6. They collect like terms to get w^2 + 5w + 6. Part C (about 5 minutes): For the Kericho plot (x + 5)(x + 3), they expand with the distributive law, getting x^2 + 3x + 5x + 15 = x^2 + 8x + 15 m^2. They then compute the fencing perimeter 2[(x + 5) + (x + 3)] = 4x + 16 m and record in a table which has an x^2 term and which does not. They test x = 5: plot is 10 m by 8 m, area 80 m^2, and 25 + 40 + 15 = 80; perimeter 4(5) + 16 = 36 m.
framework.teacherMoves: Circulate and ask: 'Which piece of your rectangle is the w squared? Show me with your finger.' Say: 'Distributive law means every term in the first bracket multiplies every term in the second bracket. How many multiplications will there be?' (4). Hold up the FOIL card (First, Outer, Inner, Last) and say: 'FOIL is a memory aid for the same four multiplications.' After Part B, pose: 'Why are 3w and 2w both in the answer, and why can we add them?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then cold-call 3 pairs. After Part C ask: 'The farmer buys wire for the fence. Which expression does she use, area or perimeter? Why is the perimeter linear while the area is quadratic?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, cold-call 2 learners. Redirect a pair that wrote x^2 + 15: 'Point to the 3x and 5x pieces in your model. Where did they go in your answer?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Concrete-Representational-Abstract progression using an area model: the physical rectangle pieces show why four products appear and why like terms combine. Comparing area and perimeter side by side (Contrasting Cases) builds understanding of why quadratic expressions differ from linear ones.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each pair's recorded steps. Indicators of understanding: (1) the pair identifies all four products in (w + 2)(w + 3) and writes w^2 + 3w + 2w + 6 before simplifying; (2) correctly combines 3w + 2w = 5w; (3) writes perimeter as 4x + 16 with no x^2 term; (4) verifies the Kericho area at x = 5 as 80 m^2. Use a quick thumbs-up/sideways/down check: 'Can you explain why 3w and 2w are like terms?' Note pairs for follow-up if fewer than 4 of 6 pairs show all four indicators.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in groups of 3-4 to expand (2x - 1)(3x + 4) without a physical model, using FOIL: First 2x x 3x = 6x^2, Outer 2x x 4 = 8x, Inner -1 x 3x = -3x, Last -1 x 4 = -4. They collect like terms to get 6x^2 + 5x - 4 and identify a = 6, b = 5, c = -4. Each group then writes a 'Why does it work?' explanation card comparing the signs in (2x - 1)(3x + 4) with those in (w + 2)(w + 3), checks the result by substituting x = 1 into both forms (1)(7) = 7 and 6 + 5 - 4 = 7, and finally works two more expansions of their own choice and swaps with another group to check. They also revisit the hall: expand w(w + 2) = w^2 + 2w, connecting to the Lesson 1 form where a = 1, b = 2 before subtracting 120, and note that the structure ax^2 + bx + c appears every time. Finally they return to the Predict sticky notes and revise their prediction with evidence.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'You have used FOIL on positive numbers. What changes when a bracket has a minus sign?' WAIT TIME: 15 seconds, then cold-call 2 groups. Listen for 'the sign stays with the term'. Prompt: 'Inner is -1 times 3x. Is that +3x or -3x? How do you know?' Display a common error, 6x^2 + 11x - 4, and ask: 'Where might this have come from? Find the mistake.' (8x + 3x instead of 8x - 3x). WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, cold-call 3 learners. Then ask: 'In all of our examples, what shape does the answer have?' Guide to ax^2 + bx + c. Ask: 'How is the Kericho area x^2 + 8x + 15 like the hall expression we met in Lesson 1?' Use a gallery walk of the groups' explanation cards for 4 minutes and ask each learner to leave one 'I agree because...' note. Return to the predictions: 'Whose prediction was close? What did we learn that changes your prediction?'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Error Analysis and Claim-Evidence-Reasoning: learners analyse a worked error, then write a claim (the expansion), evidence (substitution check), and reasoning (distributive law). Generalising across several examples helps them see the consistent structure ax^2 + bx + c, so expansion is understood and not just memorised.
framework.formativeAssessment: Collect each group's explanation card. Indicators: (1) correct expansion 6x^2 + 5x - 4; (2) correct identification of a = 6, b = 5, c = -4, with c negative; (3) a substitution check that gives equal values on both sides; (4) a written statement that the sign belongs to the term that follows it; (5) correct peer-checking of at least 1 of 2 self-chosen expansions. Use a 3-question exit ticket: expand (x + 4)(x + 1); expand (x - 2)(x + 5); state a, b, c for your answer to the second question. Success = 2 of 3 correct (expected answers x^2 + 5x + 4; x^2 + 3x - 10 with a = 1, b = 3, c = -10).

framework.learnerExperience: Learners return to the class Driving Question Board: 'How can we use quadratic equations to find unknown dimensions and quantities that help our community solve real planning problems — like building the Harambee hall in Githurai?' In pairs, they write one 'What we notice' card (for example, 'Area gives an x^2 term, perimeter does not') and one 'What we wonder' card (for example, 'If we can expand to get x^2 + 2x - 120, can we go backwards to find w?'). They post cards under the headings. The class also adds the statement on the board: 'We now know how quadratic expressions are formed.' They then sort the cards to see which questions can be answered in the next lessons.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our Githurai committee is still stuck. What have we learned today that helps them, and what do we still not know?' Give each pair 2 cards and 2 minutes to write. WAIT TIME: 10 seconds before collecting. Cold-call 4 pairs to read a card aloud and to say where to place it on the board. Point to a wonder card and say: 'If expanding turns (w + 2)(w + 3) into w^2 + 5w + 6, what would going backwards be called? We will explore that in the next lesson.' Do not answer wonder cards about solving the equation yet. Write on the board: 'We now know how quadratic expressions are formed.'
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Driving Question Board with 'What we notice / What we wonder' cards: visible tracking of growing understanding keeps the sequence coherent and lets learners' own questions (such as factorising and solving) motivate the next lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Read the cards. Indicators: (1) at least 80% of notice cards mention area/perimeter, x^2, or the pattern ax^2 + bx + c; (2) at least 3 wonder cards ask about reversing expansion or solving for w; (3) cards use correct vocabulary (expand, like terms, coefficient). If a card states 'perimeter has x^2', discuss it at the start of Lesson 3.

framework.learnerExperience: In their groups, learners add to the cumulative model poster (started in Lesson 1). Today's panel is titled 'How a quadratic expression is formed'. They draw (1) a rectangle with sides (x + 5) and (x + 3) and its area model split into x^2, 5x, 3x and 15; (2) the expansion steps with FOIL labels; (3) the result x^2 + 8x + 15 with a, b, c labelled (a = 1, b = 8, c = 15); (4) the perimeter 4x + 16 shown as linear; and (5) a connection arrow to the Githurai hall: w(w + 2) = w^2 + 2w, which becomes w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0 once the area 120 m^2 is subtracted from both sides. Under 'What we still need', they write: 'How do we go backwards from x^2 + bx + c to the brackets?' Each group member explains one part of the panel to a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Your model has to show how the expression is formed, not just the answer. Where in your drawing does the 8x come from?' WAIT TIME: 10 seconds, then cold-call 3 groups to explain one part of their poster. Prompt: 'How does the Kericho plot help the Githurai committee? What is the same about the two situations?' (Both have an area made by multiplying two lengths that include an unknown.) Ask: 'What do we still need to be able to find w = 10?' Collect responses and say: 'Next lesson we reverse the process.' Close by returning the sticky notes and asking each learner to write one sentence beginning 'I used to think ... now I think ...'.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Building: learners combine drawings, symbols and words to show how the area of a rectangle with unknown sides produces ax^2 + bx + c. Explaining their model to a peer consolidates understanding, and identifying gaps ('What we still need') links to the next lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check each poster panel. Indicators: (1) area model has the four parts correctly labelled x^2, 5x, 3x, 15; (2) expansion steps match the diagram; (3) a, b, c correctly labelled (1, 8, 15); (4) perimeter 4x + 16 correctly contrasted as linear; (5) a clear link to w(w + 2) from the Githurai hall; (6) a gap statement about reversing expansion. Success = at least 5 of 6 indicators for each group.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, reflect: Which learners confused 'adding' brackets with 'multiplying' them (for example, writing x^2 + 15)? Did the area model help them to see why four products are needed? Which learners made sign errors with negative terms such as (2x - 1), and did the error-analysis activity help? Did the 15-second wait times give quieter learners a chance to contribute, and did cold-calling feel safe? How well did learners connect the Kericho plot back to the Githurai hall? Note which learners are ready to factorise in Lesson 3 and who needs more practice with FOIL and like terms. Plan one extra mini-practice with two positive and two negative-sign expansions for those who need it.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: We observed that multiplying two brackets such as (w + 2)(w + 3) gives four products. In the area model of the Kericho plot (x + 5)(x + 3), the pieces were x^2, 5x, 3x and 15. The area x^2 + 8x + 15 m^2 has an x^2 term, but the fencing perimeter 4x + 16 m does not. At x = 5, the plot is 10 m by 8 m, with area 80 m^2 and perimeter 36 m.
summaryTablePrompt.learned: We learned to expand a product of two binomials using the distributive law and FOIL (First, Outer, Inner, Last), then collect like terms. For example, (w + 2)(w + 3) = w^2 + 5w + 6 and (2x - 1)(3x + 4) = 6x^2 + 5x - 4. The answer always has the form ax^2 + bx + c, and signs must stay with the terms that follow them.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: We can explain that the Githurai hall expression w(w + 2) and the Kericho plot area (x + 5)(x + 3) are quadratic because an unknown length is multiplied by another length that contains the unknown, creating an x^2 term. A perimeter adds lengths, so it stays linear. We now know how quadratic expressions are formed, but we still need a way to go backwards to find the brackets and later the width w of the hall.

LESSONS.title: Factorisation of Quadratic Expressions: Undoing Expansion to Find the Hidden Hall Dimensions
LESSONS.duration: 40 minutes (1 double lesson of 2 x 40 minutes recommended if time allows; core plan fits 80 minutes)
LESSONS.aresKeywords: factorise, factor pair, perfect square trinomial, difference of two squares, reverse expansion, FOIL, Githurai Harambee hall, Gikomba mandazi revenue

slo.purpose: Learners reverse the expansion process from Lesson 2 to factorise quadratic expressions of the form x^2 + bx + c and ax^2 + bx + c, including perfect square trinomials and the difference of two squares, and use this to write the Githurai hall expression w^2 + 2w - 120 as (w + 12)(w - 10).
slo.knowledge: Factorise means write an expression as a product of brackets. It is the reverse of expansion. For x^2 + bx + c we look for two numbers whose product is c and whose sum is b. Perfect square: x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2. Difference of two squares: x^2 - 49 = (x - 7)(x + 7). For ax^2 + bx + c, such as 2x^2 + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3), we split the middle term or use trial brackets and check by expanding. Hall: w^2 + 2w - 120 = (w + 12)(w - 10) using the factor pair 12 and -10 (product -120, sum 2). Gikomba mandazi: x^2 + 7x - 30 = (x + 10)(x - 3).
slo.skills: Analysing and interpreting data (finding factor pairs from a table of product and sum); using mathematics and computational thinking (reversing FOIL); constructing explanations (justifying a factorisation by expanding to check); communication and collaboration in pairs and groups.
slo.attitudes: Unity: learners work in pairs and groups to find and check factor pairs. Responsibility: learners check each other's factorisations by expanding. Appreciation that mathematics helps the community plan, as the Githurai committee does. Life skills (self-esteem): every learner contributes a factor pair or a check.
slo.keyInquiry: How do quadratic expressions and equations differ from linear ones, and why are they necessary? (KICD Key Inquiry 1) Supporting question for this lesson: How can we 'undo' expansion to find the hidden brackets inside w^2 + 2w - 120?
slo.purposeInStoryline: Lesson 1 showed that the hall gives w(w + 2) = 120, i.e. w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0, which is a quadratic equation different from a linear one. Lesson 2 taught expanding binomials with the distributive law and FOIL to get ax^2 + bx + c. Lesson 3 uses that structure in reverse: learners factorise the hall expression into (w + 12)(w - 10) and meet the Gikomba mandazi revenue expression as a new factorisation challenge. Lesson 4 will then set each factor equal to zero (Zero Product Property) to find the hall's width. This lesson stops at the factorised form and does NOT yet solve for w.
slo.safetyNotes: No hazardous materials. Use paper tiles, manila paper and markers. Keep walkways clear when learners move to the gallery wall. Pair learners so that everyone participates and no one is left out. Scissors, if used to cut algebra tiles from paper, should be blunt-ended and handled with care.

LESSONS.overview: The Githurai committee's manila-paper sketch gives the hall expression w^2 + 2w - 120, but they cannot yet see the width inside it. In this lesson learners first predict how to get back from w^2 + 2w - 120 to two brackets. They then gather evidence in the Observe phase by reversing FOIL on simple expressions (x^2 + 6x + 9, x^2 - 49, 2x^2 + 7x + 3), using a product-and-sum factor-pair table and a paper area-tile model. In the Explain phase they factorise the hall expression to (w + 12)(w - 10) and tackle the Gikomba mandazi revenue x^2 + 7x - 30 = (x + 10)(x - 3) as a challenge. They update the Driving Question Board with 'Factorisation lets us undo expansion to find hidden values' and revise the cumulative model poster. Solving for w (and rejecting -12) is left to Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners look at the committee's manila-paper sketch again (width = w, length = w + 2, Area = 120 m2) and the expression w^2 + 2w - 120 from Lesson 1. On a sticky note or in their exercise book they answer individually: 'Lesson 2 turned two brackets into one expression. If we start with w^2 + 2w - 120, how could we get back to two brackets? What do you think the two brackets might look like?' They write one prediction and one reason, e.g. 'I think the brackets are (w + something)(w - something) because the middle term is small'. They then share with a partner.
framework.teacherMoves: Display the sketch on manila paper or the board. Say: 'Yesterday we expanded (w + 2)(w + 3) to get w^2 + 5w + 6. Today the committee hands us the answer and asks for the brackets. Write your prediction silently.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'What could the brackets look like?' Give 2 minutes of silent writing, then 1 minute of pair talk. Cold-call 4 learners (not volunteers) with: 'Read your prediction and say why.' Record all predictions on the board without judging them as right or wrong. Ask: 'What would we multiply to check a prediction?' and let learners answer that expanding is the check.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Predict-Share-Revisit: learners commit to a prediction and a reason before instruction, so that later evidence can confirm or revise their thinking. Naming the check (expanding with FOIL) links Lesson 2 to this lesson and establishes the idea that factorising is the reverse of expanding.
framework.formativeAssessment: Observe whether learners: (1) write two brackets of the form (w + _)(w + _) in their prediction; (2) mention that the constant 120 or the middle term 2 must be used; (3) say that expanding checks the answer. Tally on a clipboard how many predictions use a negative sign. Learners who write only a number for w (e.g. 'w = 10') are still thinking by trial-and-error as in Lesson 1; note them for support in the Observe phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners work in pairs through three evidence stations on worksheets and with paper area tiles. Station 1 (x^2 + bx + c): they reverse FOIL on x^2 + 6x + 9. They fill a product-and-sum table: pairs with product 9 are (1, 9), (3, 3), (-1, -9), (-3, -3); the pair with sum 6 is (3, 3), giving (x + 3)(x + 3) = (x + 3)^2, a perfect square trinomial. They expand (x + 3)^2 to check. Station 2 (difference of two squares): they expand (x - 7)(x + 7) and see that the middle terms -7x and +7x cancel, giving x^2 - 49; they then factorise x^2 - 49 = (x - 7)(x + 7) and note that 49 = 7^2 and there is no x term. Station 3 (ax^2 + bx + c): for 2x^2 + 7x + 3 they find a x c = 6 and look for two numbers with product 6 and sum 7 (1 and 6), split the middle term: 2x^2 + x + 6x + 3, group: x(2x + 1) + 3(2x + 1) = (2x + 1)(x + 3), and check by FOIL. Learners record each factor-pair table in their books and use paper tiles (x^2 tile, x strips, unit squares) to build a rectangle for x^2 + 6x + 9 with sides (x + 3) and (x + 3). Each pair records: 'What we observed about the numbers in the brackets and the numbers in the expression'.
framework.teacherMoves: Set up three stations on desks or as three worksheet sections. Say: 'Your job is to be detectives. Look for a pattern between the numbers in the brackets and the numbers in the expression.' Circulate and ask each pair: 'Which two numbers multiply to give the constant? Which two add to give the middle coefficient?' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before any hint. Prompt: 'Why did the x terms disappear in x^2 - 49?' After 15 minutes, stop the class and cold-call 3 pairs, one per station: 'What pattern did you notice?' Write the three patterns on the board: product = c and sum = b; perfect square (x + 3)^2; difference of two squares (x - 7)(x + 7). Ask the class: 'Where did you see that same expansion in Lesson 2?' For learners who struggle with 2x^2 + 7x + 3, say: 'Multiply a and c first: 2 x 3 = 6. Which two numbers make 6 and add to 7?' Remind learners that every factorisation is checked by expanding.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Pattern Seeking with Reversal: learners compare the forward process (FOIL from Lesson 2) with the backward process (factorising) across three cases and generalise from the data. The factor-pair table makes the thinking visible, and the area-tile rectangle gives a concrete picture of why a perfect square has two equal sides, linking back to the rectangular hall.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) learners list factor pairs systematically, including negative pairs, in a table; (2) learners write (x + 3)(x + 3) as (x + 3)^2; (3) learners state that x^2 - 49 has no middle term because the two middle terms cancel; (4) learners check at least one factorisation by FOIL. Exit signal: ask for a thumbs up, sideways or down on 'I can find two numbers with a given product and sum'. Pairs who cannot complete the table for 2x^2 + 7x + 3 get a short mini-conference with the teacher during the Explain phase.

framework.learnerExperience: Part A, the hall: Learners return to the committee's expression w^2 + 2w - 120. In pairs they build a product-and-sum table for 120 with the constant negative: factor pairs of -120 include (10, -12), (-10, 12), (8, -15), (-8, 15), (6, -20), (-6, 20) and so on, and they look for sum +2. They find 12 and -10 (product -120, sum 2) and write w^2 + 2w - 120 = (w + 12)(w - 10). They expand with FOIL to check: w^2 - 10w + 12w - 120 = w^2 + 2w - 120. They explain in a sentence why one factor is positive and one negative. They notice that (w + 12)(w - 10) contains the numbers 10 and 12, the same numbers they saw in the trial-and-error table in Lesson 1, but they do NOT solve yet; they write 'What we wonder: How do the brackets give us the width?' Part B, the Gikomba challenge: A mandazi vendor in Gikomba, Nairobi, has (x + 3) customers each paying (x + 4) shillings, so revenue R = (x + 3)(x + 4) = x^2 + 7x + 12 KES. The vendor wants R = 42 KES, which gives x^2 + 7x - 30 (after moving 42 across). In groups of four, learners factorise x^2 + 7x - 30 by finding two numbers with product -30 and sum 7 (10 and -3), writing (x + 10)(x - 3). They check by expanding: x^2 - 3x + 10x - 30 = x^2 + 7x - 30. Each group completes the sentence: 'The steps I follow to factorise x^2 + bx + c are...' Groups then write a short comparison: how is this expression like the hall's expression, and how is it different? (Both have a negative constant; the numbers differ.) They leave the solving, and the rejection of -10, for Lesson 4.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'The committee gave us w^2 + 2w - 120. Can we now find the hidden brackets? Use your table.' Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds before taking any answer. Cold-call 3 pairs: 'Which factor pair did you choose, and how do you know the sum is 2?' Ask the class: 'Why can't 8 and -15 work?' (sum is -7) Write the factorisation on the board and have learners expand it aloud in chorus to check. Then say: 'Now the Gikomba mandazi vendor needs help. Same method, new numbers.' Circulate, asking groups: 'What is your product? What is your sum? How can you test it quickly?' Cold-call 4 groups to share their factor pair and check. Address misconceptions explicitly: (1) writing (x - 10)(x + 3) instead of (x + 10)(x - 3): ask 'Expand it. Does the middle term come out +7x or -7x?'; (2) forgetting that the sign of the larger number matches the sign of b. State clearly: 'Today we only factorise. We do not yet find w or x; that is Lesson 4.' End with: 'What is the same about the hall and the mandazi problem?' and take 2 responses.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Claim-Evidence-Reasoning with Reversal Check: learners state a claim (the factorisation), give evidence (the factor-pair table and the FOIL expansion), and give reasoning (factorising is expanding in reverse, so expanding the answer must return the original expression). Applying the same method to the hall and then to a new context (Gikomba mandazi revenue) helps learners transfer the idea rather than memorise one example.
framework.formativeAssessment: Look for: (1) the factor pair 12 and -10 chosen and justified using both product -120 and sum 2; (2) (w + 12)(w - 10) written and checked by expanding; (3) (x + 10)(x - 3) written for the mandazi expression with a correct check; (4) learners resisting the urge to solve for w and instead writing a wonder question. Quick check on mini whiteboards: 'Factorise x^2 + 5x + 6' (answer (x + 2)(x + 3)); count correct responses. Aim for at least 80% correct; if lower, reteach with the product-and-sum table before the next lesson. Collect pair work for the three tasks to identify learners needing extra support.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners add to the class Driving Question Board using 'What we notice / What we wonder' cards. Each pair writes one 'What we notice' card, for example: 'We notice that w^2 + 2w - 120 can be written as (w + 12)(w - 10)' or 'We notice that the numbers 12 and -10 multiply to -120 and add to 2'. Each pair also writes one 'What we wonder' card, for example: 'We wonder how (w + 12)(w - 10) gives the width of the hall' or 'We wonder why one number is negative and what a negative width would mean'. They place the cards on the DQB under the driving question about the Harambee hall in Githurai. The class then adds a DQB update statement: 'Factorisation lets us undo expansion to find hidden values.' Learners also note the Gikomba mandazi problem on a card: 'We wonder what x is when revenue is 42 KES'.
framework.teacherMoves: Hand out cards and say: 'Write what you noticed today and what you still wonder about the hall.' Allow 3 minutes of silent writing. Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'Which wondering cards connect to each other?' Cold-call 4 pairs to read a card and place it on the DQB. Cluster cards into themes such as 'finding the brackets', 'negative numbers', 'getting the width' and 'checking answers'. Point to the 'Factorisation lets us undo expansion to find hidden values' statement and say: 'This is our new piece of evidence. We still do not know the width. What step comes next?' Guide learners to say that each bracket might be set equal to zero, without teaching it, and tell them that Lesson 4 will investigate this. Ask: 'Which wonder cards did today's lesson answer, and which are new?' and move answered cards to a 'We have learned' strip.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Question Clustering on the DQB: learners link new observations to the unresolved driving question, track what is answered and unanswered, and see the lesson as one step in a longer investigation. This keeps the Githurai hall as the thread that connects every lesson.
framework.formativeAssessment: Check that at least 80% of pairs submit one 'notice' and one 'wonder' card. Look for notice cards that mention the factor pair (12 and -10) or the reverse of expansion, and wonder cards that show a genuine next step (e.g. how to get w from the brackets). Note any cards that show a misconception, such as 'w = 12 because of the 12 in the bracket', and address them at the start of Lesson 4.

framework.learnerExperience: Learners update the cumulative model poster for the Harambee hall, which in earlier lessons showed the hall sketch, the equation w(w + 2) = 120 and the expanded form w^2 + 2w - 120 = 0. In groups of four they add a new panel titled 'Factorising: undoing expansion'. The panel contains: (1) a two-way arrow diagram, with 'expand (FOIL)' going from (w + 12)(w - 10) to w^2 + 2w - 120 and 'factorise' going back; (2) the factor-pair table for 120 with the pair 12 and -10 circled; (3) the three patterns from the Observe phase, x^2 + 6x + 9 = (x + 3)^2, x^2 - 49 = (x - 7)(x + 7) and 2x^2 + 7x + 3 = (2x + 1)(x + 3); (4) the Gikomba mandazi example x^2 + 7x - 30 = (x + 10)(x - 3). Each group writes one sentence at the bottom: 'Factorising helps the Githurai committee because...' and adds a placeholder box 'Next: use the brackets to find w' for Lesson 4. Finally, learners complete the three-column summary table (see below) in their books.
framework.teacherMoves: Say: 'Our model poster must show how we got from the sketch to the brackets. Add a panel that someone from another school could follow.' Provide manila paper and markers (in the same spirit as the committee's sketch). Give WAIT TIME of 10-15 seconds after asking: 'How is factorising linked to expanding in the diagram?' Circulate and ask each group: 'Where does the 12 come from? Why is -10 negative?' Cold-call 3 groups to present their arrow diagram in 30 seconds each; ask the class to give one 'star' (what is clear) and one 'step' (what could be clearer). Remind learners: 'We have not yet found the width. Write that on your poster as the next step.' Close with a whole-class check: 'Hands up if you can factorise w^2 + 2w - 120 without notes.' Collect the summary tables as an exit ticket.
framework.sensemakingStrategy: Cumulative Model Revision: learners extend a visible, shared model of the hall problem by adding the new relationship (expanding and factorising as inverse processes). Representing the idea as a diagram, a table and worked examples builds a multi-representation understanding and records the progress of the class thinking across lessons.
framework.formativeAssessment: Use a checklist for each group poster: (1) two-way expand/factorise diagram present and correct; (2) factor pair 12 and -10 shown with product -120 and sum 2; (3) at least one perfect square or difference of two squares example correct; (4) Gikomba example (x + 10)(x - 3) correct; (5) next-step placeholder for finding w. Exit ticket: 'Factorise x^2 + 7x + 12 and check by expanding' (answer (x + 3)(x + 4), the Gikomba revenue before the target is applied). Learners who miss the check step are given extra practice at the start of Lesson 4.

LESSONS.teacherReflection: After the lesson, ask yourself: (1) Did every learner use the product-and-sum table, or did some still rely on trial-and-error guessing as in the Lesson 1 predictions? (2) Which sign errors appeared most often (for example (x - 10)(x + 3) written for (x + 10)(x - 3)), and did expanding help learners find and fix them? (3) Could learners explain why factorising is the reverse of expanding in their own words, using the hall as an example? (4) Did anyone start solving for w too early, and what does this tell me about readiness for Lesson 4? (5) Which cards on the DQB show the most curiosity, and how can I use them to open the next lesson? (6) How well did the Gikomba mandazi context hold learner interest compared with the hall? Note which learners need more practice with ax^2 + bx + c, and plan a short warm-up using 2x^2 + 7x + 3 at the start of Lesson 4.

summaryTablePrompt.observed: What did we observe? Example: When we reversed FOIL, the two numbers in the brackets multiplied to give the constant and added to give the middle coefficient. x^2 + 6x + 9 became (x + 3)^2, x^2 - 49 became (x - 7)(x + 7), and 2x^2 + 7x + 3 became (2x + 1)(x + 3).
summaryTablePrompt.learned: What did we learn? Example: Factorising means writing an expression as a product of brackets, and it is the reverse of expanding. We can always check a factorisation by expanding it. Perfect squares and the difference of two squares are special patterns.
summaryTablePrompt.explained: How does this help explain the Githurai hall? Example: The hall expression w^2 + 2w - 120 factorises as (w + 12)(w - 10) using the factor pair 12 and -10 (product -120, sum 2). The same method works for the Gikomba mandazi revenue x^2 + 7x - 30 = (x + 10)(x - 3). We have the hidden brackets, but we still wonder how they give the width; that is the next step.
